About 20% of new customers return the next month

Cohort retention

Rows: first purchase month · Columns: months since first purchase. The Dec-2009 cohort includes long-standing customers because the data starts that month, so it is not used as the retention benchmark.

Key findings

  • Seasonality
    Sales climb from September and peak in November: £1.43M in 2010 and £1.45M in 2011. Growth came almost entirely from the peak season.
  • Cancellations
    The jump to 4.8% in 2011 came from just two orders. Without them the cancellation rate is a stable 2.3–2.5%.
  • Products
    22% of products generate 80% of revenue, led by cake stands, T-light holders and party bunting.
  • Customers
    901 At Risk and Can't Lose Them customers once spent £1.73M (10% of revenue) and have gone quiet.
  • Retention
    About 20% of new customers buy again the next month. December buyers return least (9%), likely one-off Christmas shoppers.

Recommendation

Protect Champions with a loyalty program and early access to the seasonal range. Run a win-back campaign for At Risk and Can't Lose Them customers before the September peak, and add a 30-day second-order offer, with a January follow-up for December buyers.

Process

View on GitHub
  1. CleanPower Query on 1M+ rows (beyond the sheet limit), with a step-by-step cleaning log.
  2. ModelPower Pivot data model, Calendar table and 9 DAX measures (AOV, cancellation rate, MoM).
  3. AnalysePivot tables for trend, Pareto and cancellations; found and removed two anomalous orders.
  4. SegmentRFM scores with PERCENTRANK.INC and a two-way XLOOKUP segment map.
  5. Retain and presentCohort retention heatmap and a dashboard with slicers.

Late Deliveries at Olist

What makes deliveries arrive after the promised date, and does lateness lower customer ratings?

Arrived late8.11%7,826 of 96,478 orders

Key findings

  • Ratings
    On-time orders average 4.29 stars, late orders 2.57.
  • Tolerance
    Up to 3 days late still averages 3.59; at 4–7 days the 1-star share jumps from 18% to 59%.
  • Volume
    Black Friday had the most orders, but Feb–Mar 2018 had the highest late rates: slower delivery, tight estimates.
  • Distance
    64% of orders ship across states and are late 9.3% vs 6.1% of the time.
  • Region
    About 60% of sellers are in São Paulo; the far Northeast is late 14.3% of the time.

Recommendation

Set delivery estimates by route, based on recent actual delivery times between the seller's and the customer's state, starting with cross-state orders and the Northeast. Track delivery time per route every month as an early warning.

Process

View on GitHub
  1. Import and validate5 MySQL tables; fixed a merged review row and a duplicate load.
  2. ExploreMonthly late rate, estimated vs actual delivery time.
  3. Join and compare4-table joins without double-counting orders.
  4. Trends and rankingLAG and RANK with PARTITION BY.
  5. Dashboard and write-upPower BI with DAX; README on GitHub.

Presence Insight

How often are employees on site, working from home or on sick leave?

Presence91.83%overall presence rate
Work from home10.00%of working days

What I did

  1. Clean the dataUnpivoted daily attendance codes and fixed data types in Power Query.
  2. Build measuresDAX measures for presence, WFH and sick-leave rates.
  3. Design the reportRate cards, daily trends, weekday tables and a month slicer.

What the dashboard shows

  • Weekday
    Presence is highest on Monday (93.2%) and lowest on Friday (90.2%).
  • Remote
    Friday has the highest WFH rate (13.0%), so the Friday dip is mostly remote work, not absence.
